comm.t: King Suratha, listening with the merchant Samādhi in the hermitage of the sage Medhas, interrupts the narrative after the death of Raktabīja (end of chapter 8) to ask what happened next. In recitation the chapter opens with ॐ, a bīja of the pāṭha and not a word of the verse.

sandhi.note: Final m before a consonant is written as anusvāra. Before a vowel it simply joins: विचित्रमिदमाख्यातं.
Visarga before c becomes s, and the s becomes the palatal ś next to the palatal c.

samasa.sense: the glory shown in what the Devī did
samasa.alt: Also possible as a samāhāra dvandva, चरितं च माहात्म्यं च, ‘the deeds and the greatness’ (hence the neuter singular). The tatpuruṣa fits the title of the work, देवीमाहात्म्य, better.

samasa.type: dvitīyā tatpuruṣa (its first member रक्तबीजवध is a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa: रक्तबीजस्य वधः)
samasa.literal: resting on the slaying of Raktabīja

samasa.sense: the asura from each drop of whose blood another like him arose (chapter 8)

morph.note: Past passive participle used as the main verb, with the agent in the instrumental (भवता): ‘has been told by you’.
Vocative of भगवत्; the nominative is भगवान्. A form of address to a sage or god.
Instrumental of भवत्, the polite ‘you’, which takes third-person verbs; here the agent of a passive participle.

mantras.anvaya: भगवन्, भवता मम इदं रक्तबीजवधाश्रितं देव्याः चरितमाहात्म्यं विचित्रम् आख्यातम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A passive sentence: the subject चरितमाहात्म्यम् with its qualifiers, the participle आख्यातम् as verb, भवता the agent and मम the hearer; विचित्रम् is predicative.
mantras.lit: Wonderful is this that has been told to me by you, O venerable one: the greatness of the Devī’s deeds, connected with the slaying of Raktabīja.
mantras.tr: Holy sir, what you have told me is wonderful: the glory of the Goddess’s deeds in the slaying of Raktabīja.

comm.t: Suratha sums up chapter 8 — the Devī and the Mothers against Raktabīja, whose every drop of blood became a new asura until Kālī drank it — and calls it विचित्र, ‘marvellous’.

The question keeps the frame of the text alive: the third (uttama) carita, like the first two, is told as Medhas’s answer to the king. The Gita Press pāṭha assigns this carita to Mahāsarasvatī as its presiding form; that is liturgical tradition, not a statement of the verse.

sandhi.note: Visarga before c → s → ś. The same change gives निशुम्भश्च.
a + i → e (चेच्छामि); final i before a becomes y (इच्छाम्यहम्). The cch belongs to the present stem इच्छ- itself.
-aḥ before the voiced y becomes -o. यत् before k is unchanged (an unvoiced stop before an unvoiced consonant) and is only written together.
-aḥ c- → -aśc-; then च + अति → चाति (a + a → ā).

samasa.type: prādi tatpuruṣa (the prefix अति as first member)

morph.note: Present of √इष् ‘to wish’: the tudādi present stem is इच्छ-. With the infinitive श्रोतुम्: ‘I wish to hear’.
Past participle of the causative पातय- with नि: ‘made to fall, felled’. In the locative with रक्तबीजे it forms a locative absolute: ‘Raktabīja having been felled’.
Perfect of √कृ (reduplicated च-कार). Singular with two subjects: it agrees with शुम्भः, and निशुम्भश्च is added after, a common pattern.

mantras.anvaya: रक्तबीजे निपातिते शुम्भः अतिकोपनः निशुम्भः च यत् कर्म चकार, (तत्) अहं भूयः च श्रोतुम् इच्छामि।
mantras.anvaya_en: The main clause (अहं … श्रोतुम् इच्छामि) takes as its object a relative clause (यत् कर्म चकार …); the correlative तत् is supplied. रक्तबीजे निपातिते is a locative absolute giving the time.
mantras.lit: And further I wish to hear what deed Śumbha did, and the exceedingly wrathful Niśumbha, when Raktabīja had been felled.
mantras.tr: I wish to hear more: once Raktabīja had been struck down, what did Śumbha do, and Niśumbha in his towering rage?
mantras.tr_note: The relative clause is turned into a question for natural English.

comm.t: Suratha asks for the sequel: the deeds of the two brothers, Śumbha and Niśumbha, the lords of the asuras whose generals have now all fallen. Chapter 9 answers for Niśumbha; chapter 10 for Śumbha.

A modern reading: the king asks to hear ‘more’ (भूयः). In this text listening is not idle — the whole Māhātmya is offered as something heard, and the hearing itself is what transforms Suratha and Samādhi.

comm.t: Medhas, the forest sage, answers Suratha. From here to the end of the chapter (9.41) the narrative is his.

morph.note: With कोपम्, ‘made anger’ = became angry, a common idiom (cf. शुम्भः कोपं परं ययौ, 9.23). The singular agrees with the first subject, शुम्भासुरः.
Past participle of √हन् (हत), locative plural in a second locative absolute: ‘the others having been slain’.

mantras.anvaya: रक्तबीजे निपातिते आहवे अन्येषु च हतेषु शुम्भासुरः निशुम्भः च अतुलं कोपं चकार।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two locative absolutes (रक्तबीजे निपातिते; अन्येषु हतेषु) set the scene; the main clause is शुम्भासुरः निशुम्भः च … कोपं चकार.
mantras.lit: Raktabīja having been felled, and the others having been slain in battle, the asura Śumbha and Niśumbha made immeasurable anger.
mantras.tr: With Raktabīja struck down and the others slain in battle, the asura Śumbha and Niśumbha flew into a rage beyond all measure.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Made anger’ (कोपं चकार) is rendered idiomatically as ‘flew into a rage’.

comm.t: Medhas answers the king’s question at once: the loss of Raktabīja and the rest of the army drives both brothers to fury. The asura commanders of the uttama carita — Dhūmralocana, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, Raktabīja — have now all fallen; only the two lords remain.
A modern reading: the text repeatedly shows anger rising as defeat closes in. The rage of the brothers is not strength but the last form their pride takes.
